class-11/chemistry/chemical-bonding-and-.centralConcept: Octet theory — why atoms bond at all

subtopics.name: Shells and valence electrons
points: Electrons occupy shells K, L, M, N at increasing distance and energy
Valence electrons are those in the outermost shell — they decide chemical behaviour
Valency is the combining capacity, equal to electrons gained, lost or shared to reach an octet

subtopics.name: The octet rule
points: Atoms tend to attain eight electrons in the outermost shell, matching the noble gas configuration
Kossel and Lewis proposed it independently in 1916
Noble gases are already stable, which is why they rarely bond

branches.topic: Level 2 — Core: how the octet is achieved

subtopics.name: Three routes to an octet
points: Transfer of electrons — ionic bonding (metal loses, non-metal gains)
Sharing of electrons — covalent bonding (both contribute)
Coordination — one atom donates a lone pair to another

subtopics.name: Lewis structures
points: Dots represent valence electrons; a shared pair is a bond
Total valence electrons must be conserved when drawing
Formal charge helps decide between competing structures

branches.topic: Level 3 — Upgraded: where the octet rule fails

subtopics.name: Exceptions
points: Incomplete octet: BeCl2 (4 electrons), BF3 (6 electrons), LiCl
Expanded octet: PCl5 (10), SF6 (12) — possible only for period 3 and below with accessible d orbitals
Odd-electron species: NO and NO2 have unpaired electrons and cannot satisfy an octet

subtopics.name: Why it still matters
points: The octet rule is a useful first approximation, not a law
Molecular orbital theory is needed for O2 paramagnetism, which the octet picture cannot explain
Hydrogen obeys a duet rule, not an octet

class-11/chemistry/chemical-bonding-and-.centralConcept: Ionic bonding — electrostatic attraction after electron transfer

subtopics.name: Electron transfer
points: A metal with low ionisation energy loses electrons to form a cation
A non-metal with high electron affinity gains them to form an anion
The ions are held by electrostatic attraction in a giant lattice

subtopics.name: Energetics
points: Lattice enthalpy is the energy released when gaseous ions form the solid
Born-Haber cycle accounts for the full energy balance
High lattice enthalpy means a high melting point

subtopics.name: Physical properties
points: High melting and boiling points — strong electrostatic forces must be broken
Hard and brittle — a shift brings like charges together and the crystal cleaves
Usually soluble in polar solvents such as water, insoluble in non-polar solvents

subtopics.name: Electrical behaviour
points: Solid does not conduct — ions are locked in the lattice
Molten or aqueous state conducts — ions become mobile
This is the classic test distinguishing ionic from covalent compounds

subtopics.name: Fajans' rules
points: Small, highly charged cations polarise anions strongly, adding covalent character
LiCl and BeCl2 are more covalent than NaCl and MgCl2 for this reason
No bond is purely ionic — all have some covalent character

subtopics.name: Real examples
points: NaCl: melting point 801 degrees Celsius, conducts when molten
MgO: very high lattice enthalpy, melting point ~2852 degrees Celsius
Ionic liquids are salts molten near room temperature — a modern exception

class-11/chemistry/chemical-bonding-and-.centralConcept: Covalent bonding — sharing electrons to complete an octet

subtopics.name: Formation
points: Two atoms each contribute one electron to a shared pair
The shared pair is attracted to both nuclei, lowering the energy
Bond order one is a single bond; two and three are double and triple

subtopics.name: Bond length and strength
points: Shorter bond generally means stronger bond
Triple shorter and stronger than double, which is shorter and stronger than single
C-C 154 pm, C=C 134 pm, C triple bond C 120 pm

branches.topic: Level 2 — Core: coordinate bonding and properties

subtopics.name: Coordinate (dative) covalent bond
points: One atom donates both electrons of the shared pair; the other supplies none
The donor must have a lone pair; the acceptor an empty orbital
Examples: NH4+, H3O+, and the coordinate bonds in metal complexes

subtopics.name: Properties of covalent compounds
points: Low melting and boiling points for simple molecular substances — weak intermolecular forces
Generally poor conductors — no free ions or electrons
Usually soluble in non-polar solvents, insoluble in water unless they can hydrogen-bond

subtopics.name: Network solids are the exception
points: Diamond, graphite, silicon dioxide and silicon carbide are giant covalent lattices
Very high melting points because covalent bonds must be broken, not just intermolecular forces
Graphite conducts because of delocalised electrons between layers; diamond does not

subtopics.name: Bond polarity
points: A bond between different elements is polar unless the electronegativity difference is zero
Electronegativity difference above roughly 1.7 gives predominantly ionic character
Polar bonds may or may not give a polar molecule — symmetry decides

class-11/chemistry/chemical-bonding-and-.centralConcept: Covalent and coordinate bonds and the properties they produce

subtopics.name: Sharing versus donation
points: Ordinary covalent: each atom contributes one electron
Coordinate covalent: one atom contributes both
Once formed, a coordinate bond is indistinguishable from an ordinary covalent bond

subtopics.name: Properties
points: Simple molecular compounds: low melting point, soft, volatile
Non-conducting in all states unless they ionise in water
Intermolecular forces, not covalent bonds, are broken on melting

subtopics.name: Coordinate bond examples
points: NH3 + H+ gives NH4+ — nitrogen donates its lone pair
H2O + H+ gives H3O+
Carbon monoxide has a coordinate bond from oxygen to carbon

subtopics.name: Consequences
points: Coordinate bonding explains why NH4+ salts behave like ionic compounds despite a covalent cation
Ligand bonding in complexes is coordinate bonding
Giant covalent solids break the low-melting-point generalisation

class-11/chemistry/chemical-bonding-and-.centralConcept: Lewis structures — drawing where the electrons are

subtopics.name: Step-by-step construction
points: Count total valence electrons from all atoms, adjusting for charge
Connect atoms with single bonds, then place remaining electrons as lone pairs
Form multiple bonds if an octet is still incomplete

subtopics.name: Formal charge
points: Formal charge = valence electrons - (lone pair electrons/2) - bonds
The structure with formal charges closest to zero is preferred
Negative formal charge belongs on the more electronegative atom

branches.topic: Level 2 — Core: s and p block examples

subtopics.name: Common structures
points: H2O: two O-H bonds plus two lone pairs on oxygen, bent
NH3: three N-H bonds plus one lone pair, pyramidal
CO2: two double bonds, linear, no lone pairs on carbon

subtopics.name: Expanded octet cases
points: PCl5 has five bonding pairs on phosphorus — 10 electrons
SF6 has six bonding pairs on sulfur — 12 electrons
Only period 3 elements and below can expand their octet

subtopics.name: Resonance structures
points: When more than one valid Lewis structure exists, the real molecule is a hybrid
Ozone and carbonate ion are standard examples
Resonance stabilises the molecule by delocalising electrons

subtopics.name: Limits of the Lewis model
points: Cannot explain O2 paramagnetism
Gives no information about bond angles or three-dimensional shape
Molecular orbital theory is required for these

class-11/chemistry/chemical-bonding-and-.centralConcept: VSEPR — electron pairs repel and set the shape

subtopics.name: The principle
points: Valence Shell Electron Pair Repulsion theory: electron pairs around a central atom arrange to minimise repulsion
Lone pairs repel more strongly than bond pairs
Multiple bonds repel more strongly than single bonds

branches.topic: Level 2 — Core: geometries by electron-pair number

subtopics.name: Two to four pairs
points: 2 pairs: linear, 180 degrees (BeCl2, CO2)
3 pairs: trigonal planar, 120 degrees (BF3); one lone pair gives bent ~119 degrees (SO2)
4 pairs: tetrahedral, 109.5 degrees (CH4); one lone pair gives pyramidal ~107 degrees (NH3); two lone pairs give bent ~104.5 degrees (H2O)

subtopics.name: Five and six pairs
points: 5 pairs: trigonal bipyramidal (PCl5); lone pairs occupy equatorial positions (SF4 seesaw, ClF3 T-shaped)
6 pairs: octahedral (SF6); lone pairs give square pyramidal (BrF5) or square planar (XeF4)
Lone pairs always take the position that minimises repulsion

subtopics.name: Why angles shrink
points: Repulsion order: lone pair-lone pair > lone pair-bond pair > bond pair-bond pair
Each lone pair compresses the bond angle by roughly 2 to 3 degrees
CH4 109.5 > NH3 107 > H2O 104.5 is the standard demonstration

subtopics.name: Limitations
points: VSEPR predicts shape, not bond energy or magnetic behaviour
Fails for some transition metal compounds where d electrons matter
Does not explain why a shape is stable, only that it is least repulsive

class-11/chemistry/chemical-bonding-and-.centralConcept: Predicting molecular shape from electron-pair repulsion

subtopics.name: Steric number
points: Steric number = bonding pairs + lone pairs on the central atom
The steric number sets the electron geometry; lone pairs then modify the molecular shape
Always draw the Lewis structure first

subtopics.name: No lone pairs
points: BeF2: 2 pairs, linear, 180 degrees
BF3: 3 pairs, trigonal planar, 120 degrees
CH4: 4 pairs, tetrahedral, 109.5 degrees
PCl5: 5 pairs, trigonal bipyramidal; SF6: 6 pairs, octahedral

subtopics.name: With lone pairs
points: H2O: 4 pairs, 2 lone, bent, 104.5 degrees
NH3: 4 pairs, 1 lone, pyramidal, 107 degrees
H2S: bent, ~92 degrees — smaller than water because sulfur is less electronegative
PH3: pyramidal, ~93.5 degrees

subtopics.name: Special cases
points: CO2: two double bonds, linear, 180 degrees
CH3Cl: tetrahedral geometry, but the molecule is polar because of the C-Cl bond
Multiple bonds count as one electron domain for geometry

subtopics.name: Symmetry decides polarity
points: CO2 has polar bonds but is non-polar — the two dipoles cancel
H2O has polar bonds and is polar — the bent shape leaves a net dipole
CCl4 is non-polar while CHCl3 is polar, purely because of symmetry

class-11/chemistry/chemical-bonding-and-.centralConcept: Hybridization — mixing orbitals to explain real geometry

subtopics.name: The problem
points: Carbon's ground state has two unpaired electrons, predicting only two bonds, yet it forms four
Pure s and p orbitals would give unequal bond angles, which is not observed
Hybridization mixes orbitals of similar energy to give equivalent new orbitals

subtopics.name: Definition
points: Hybrid orbitals have identical shape and energy, directed to minimise repulsion
Number of hybrid orbitals equals the number of atomic orbitals mixed
Hybridization is a model, not a physical process that can be observed

subtopics.name: sp3, sp2, sp
points: sp3: one s + three p, four orbitals, tetrahedral, 109.5 degrees (CH4, NH3, H2O)
sp2: one s + two p, three orbitals, trigonal planar, 120 degrees, leaves one p for a pi bond (C2H4)
sp: one s + one p, two orbitals, linear, 180 degrees, leaves two p for two pi bonds (C2H2)

subtopics.name: Steric number link
points: Steric number 4 gives sp3; 3 gives sp2; 2 gives sp
Lone pairs occupy hybrid orbitals and affect shape but not the hybridization label
Water is sp3 hybridized although its molecular shape is bent

subtopics.name: Bond length and strength
points: More s character means a shorter, stronger bond
sp has 50% s character, sp2 33%, sp3 25%
C-H bond length: sp 106 pm < sp2 108 pm < sp3 109 pm

subtopics.name: Pi bonding and rotation
points: Unhybridized p orbitals form pi bonds by sideways overlap
Pi bonds prevent free rotation, which is why alkenes show cis-trans isomerism
A double bond is one sigma plus one pi; a triple bond is one sigma plus two pi

class-11/chemistry/chemical-bonding-and-.centralConcept: sp, sp2 and sp3 hybridization in organic molecules

subtopics.name: Sigma and pi frames
points: Sigma bonds form by head-on overlap and lie along the internuclear axis
Pi bonds form by sideways overlap and lie above and below the axis
Only unhybridized p orbitals can form pi bonds

subtopics.name: Worked assignments
points: Ethane C2H6: both carbons sp3, all single bonds, free rotation
Ethene C2H4: both carbons sp2, one pi bond, planar, no rotation
Ethyne C2H2: both carbons sp, two pi bonds, linear

subtopics.name: Mixed examples
points: Benzene: every carbon sp2, giving a planar ring with delocalised pi electrons
Acetaldehyde CH3CHO: CH3 carbon sp3, carbonyl carbon sp2
Carbon dioxide: carbon sp hybridized, two pi bonds

subtopics.name: Reading hybridization from structure
points: Count sigma bonds plus lone pairs on the atom — that is the steric number
An atom with one double bond and two single bonds is sp2
Hybridization explains geometry; geometry does not explain hybridization

class-11/chemistry/chemical-bonding-and-.centralConcept: Valence bond theory — bonds as overlapping orbitals

subtopics.name: The central claim
points: A covalent bond forms when two half-filled orbitals overlap
Greater overlap means a stronger bond
The two electrons must have opposite spins to pair

subtopics.name: Types of overlap
points: s-s overlap: H2
s-p overlap: HCl
p-p head-on overlap gives sigma; p-p sideways overlap gives pi

subtopics.name: Strengths and limits
points: Sigma overlap is more effective than pi, so sigma bonds are stronger
VBT explains geometry through hybridization
VBT cannot explain the paramagnetism of oxygen

subtopics.name: Where VBT falls short
points: O2 is predicted diamagnetic by VBT but is actually paramagnetic
Cannot explain the detailed electronic spectra of complexes
Molecular orbital theory was developed to fix exactly these failures

class-11/chemistry/chemical-bonding-and-.centralConcept: Molecular orbital theory — electrons belong to the whole molecule

subtopics.name: Atomic to molecular orbitals
points: Atomic orbitals combine to give molecular orbitals spanning the whole molecule
Combining n atomic orbitals gives n molecular orbitals
Bonding MOs are lower in energy; antibonding MOs are higher and marked with a star

subtopics.name: Bond order
points: Bond order = (bonding electrons - antibonding electrons) / 2
Bond order zero means the molecule does not exist (He2)
Higher bond order means shorter, stronger bond

subtopics.name: Magnetic behaviour
points: Unpaired electrons in an MO make the species paramagnetic
O2 has two unpaired electrons in pi-star orbitals, so it is paramagnetic — VBT fails here
N2 has bond order 3 and is diamagnetic

subtopics.name: Explaining the unexplainable
points: O2 paramagnetism, and why O2+ has a higher bond order than O2
Why NO is paramagnetic while NO+ is not
H2+ exists with bond order 0.5, which no Lewis structure can describe

subtopics.name: Limits
points: MO theory is mathematically heavier than VBT
For most organic molecules VBT plus hybridization is sufficient and simpler
Both models are approximations of the same quantum reality

class-11/chemistry/chemical-bonding-and-.centralConcept: Resonance — one real structure, several drawings

subtopics.name: Definition
points: Resonance describes a molecule for which more than one valid Lewis structure can be drawn
The real molecule is a hybrid of all contributing structures, not any one of them
Double-headed arrow links the contributing structures

subtopics.name: Rules for valid contributors
points: Only electrons move — atomic positions stay fixed
Contributors must have the same number of paired electrons
The more covalent bonds and the fewer formal charges, the more stable the contributor

subtopics.name: Standard examples
points: Ozone O3: two equivalent contributors, bond order 1.5
Carbonate CO3 2-: three equivalent contributors, all C-O bonds equal
Benzene: two Kekule structures, all six C-C bonds identical at 139 pm

subtopics.name: Stabilisation
points: Resonance delocalises electrons and lowers the energy — this is resonance stabilisation
Explains why benzene does not behave like an alkene
Explains the acidity of carboxylic acids: the conjugate base is resonance stabilised

subtopics.name: Bond order
points: Resonance bond order = total bonds / number of resonance positions
Benzene C-C bond order is 1.5, between single and double
Explains intermediate bond lengths that match neither single nor double

class-11/chemistry/chemical-bonding-and-.centralConcept: Bond characteristics — measuring what a bond is like

branches.topic: Level 1 — Foundation: bond length and order

subtopics.name: Bond length
points: The equilibrium distance between two bonded nuclei
Increases with atomic size, decreases with bond order
Measured in picometres (pm) or angstroms

subtopics.name: Bond order and energy
points: Bond order is the number of electron pairs shared
Higher bond order gives shorter, stronger bonds
Bond dissociation energy is the energy needed to break one mole of bonds

subtopics.name: Dipole moment
points: Dipole moment mu = charge x distance, measured in debye (D)
A polar bond has a non-zero dipole moment
A symmetric molecule can have polar bonds but zero net dipole moment

subtopics.name: Ionic character
points: Percentage ionic character = (observed dipole / calculated for full charge) x 100
HF is about 43% ionic character despite being called a covalent molecule
Electronegativity difference drives ionic character

branches.topic: Level 3 — Upgraded: bond angle and comparisons

subtopics.name: Bond angle
points: The angle between two bonds at the central atom
Lone pair repulsion compresses bond angles
Hybridization sets the base angle: sp 180, sp2 120, sp3 109.5

subtopics.name: Ordering questions
points: Bond length order: single > double > triple
Bond strength order: triple > double > single
Dipole moment: NH3 > NF3 because the lone pair and bond dipoles reinforce in NH3

class-11/chemistry/chemical-bonding-and-.centralConcept: Metallic bonding — a sea of delocalised electrons

subtopics.name: The electron sea model
points: Metal atoms release their valence electrons into a common pool
Positive metal ions sit in a lattice surrounded by mobile electrons
Attraction between ions and the electron sea holds the solid together

subtopics.name: Physical properties
points: Good conductors of heat and electricity — free electrons carry charge and energy
Malleable and ductile — layers can slide without breaking the bonding
Lustrous because free electrons absorb and re-emit light

subtopics.name: Melting points
points: Vary widely: mercury is liquid at room temperature, tungsten melts at 3422 degrees Celsius
Strength depends on the number of delocalised electrons and nuclear charge
Group 1 metals are soft and low-melting; transition metals are hard and high-melting

subtopics.name: From sea to bands
points: Band theory: overlapping atomic orbitals form continuous energy bands
Conductors have a partly filled band; insulators have a large band gap
Semiconductors have a small gap and conduct when thermally excited

subtopics.name: Alloys
points: Adding a different-sized atom distorts layers and increases hardness
Steel, brass and bronze are substitutional or interstitial alloys
Explains why alloys are harder than pure metals

class-11/chemistry/chemical-bonding-and-.centralConcept: Intermolecular forces — the weak forces that decide physical state

subtopics.name: Strength order
points: Hydrogen bond > dipole-dipole > London dispersion forces
All are far weaker than covalent bonds, typically under 40 kJ/mol
They determine melting point, boiling point and solubility, not molecular identity

subtopics.name: London dispersion forces
points: Instantaneous dipole-induced dipole attraction present in all molecules
Strength increases with the number of electrons and surface area
Explains why boiling point rises down a noble gas group

subtopics.name: Conditions
points: Hydrogen must be covalently bonded to a highly electronegative N, O or F
The H becomes strongly positive and attracts a lone pair on a neighbouring atom
Typical energy 10-40 kJ/mol, much stronger than other intermolecular forces

subtopics.name: Consequences
points: Water boils at 100 degrees Celsius, far above H2S at -60 degrees Celsius
Ice is less dense than water because the hydrogen-bonded lattice is open
Ethanol is miscible with water while ethane is not

subtopics.name: Biological and material roles
points: DNA base pairing (A-T two bonds, G-C three bonds) and protein secondary structure
Hydrogen bonding in nylon and in cellulose gives strength and water absorption
Anomalous properties of water: high specific heat, high surface tension, high latent heat

subtopics.name: Intramolecular vs intermolecular
points: Intramolecular hydrogen bonding (as in ortho-nitrophenol) lowers boiling point
Intermolecular hydrogen bonding (as in para-nitrophenol) raises it
This is a classic exam distinction

subtopics.name: Two mechanisms
points: Ionic: complete transfer of electrons, giving discrete ions
Covalent: sharing of electron pairs between atoms
The choice depends on ionisation energy and electron affinity

subtopics.name: Contrasting properties
points: Ionic compounds: high melting point, conduct when molten, usually water-soluble
Covalent compounds: low melting point, non-conducting, usually non-polar solvents
Ionic bonds form between metal and non-metal; covalent between non-metals

subtopics.name: The continuum
points: Bonding is a continuum, not a binary
Electronegativity difference above ~1.7 gives predominantly ionic character
Below that, the bond is polar covalent

subtopics.name: Intermediate cases
points: HF has significant ionic character yet is a covalent molecule
BeCl2 is covalent despite being metal plus non-metal, because of high polarising power
Fajans' rules predict the drift toward covalency

class-11/chemistry/classification-of-ele.centralConcept: Modern periodic law — properties are periodic functions of atomic number

branches.topic: Level 1 — Foundation: from Mendeleev to Moseley

subtopics.name: Mendeleev's law and its problem
points: Mendeleev arranged elements by atomic mass and left gaps for undiscovered elements
Some pairs were out of order — tellurium and iodine — because mass order conflicts with chemical behaviour
The anomaly was resolved by atomic number

subtopics.name: Moseley's contribution
points: Moseley (1913) showed that the frequency of X-rays emitted depends on nuclear charge
This established atomic number as the fundamental ordering principle
Modern periodic law: properties are periodic functions of atomic number

branches.topic: Level 2 — Core: structure of the table

subtopics.name: Periods and groups
points: Seven periods; period number equals the outermost principal quantum number
Eighteen groups in the long form; group number relates to valence electrons
Elements in a group share valence configuration and therefore similar chemistry

subtopics.name: Blocks
points: s-block: groups 1 and 2, filling s orbitals
p-block: groups 13 to 18, filling p orbitals
d-block: transition metals; f-block: lanthanides and actinides

branches.topic: Level 3 — Upgraded: why the table works

subtopics.name: Electronic basis
points: Periodicity arises because valence configuration repeats after each noble gas
Chemical properties are determined almost entirely by valence electrons
The table is a map of electron configurations, not just a list

class-11/chemistry/classification-of-ele.centralConcept: Periodic trends — how size, energy and character change

subtopics.name: Across a period
points: Nuclear charge increases while electrons enter the same shell
Effective nuclear charge rises, so the atom contracts
Atomic radius decreases left to right

subtopics.name: Down a group
points: A new shell is added each period
Shielding increases faster than nuclear charge
Atomic radius increases down the group

subtopics.name: Ionisation energy and electron affinity
points: Ionisation energy increases across a period, decreases down a group
Electron affinity becomes more negative across a period
Exceptions: Be > B and N > O in ionisation energy, due to filled or half-filled subshells

subtopics.name: Electronegativity and metallic character
points: Electronegativity increases across a period, decreases down a group
Fluorine is the most electronegative element at 3.98
Metallic character decreases across a period, increases down a group

subtopics.name: Why anomalies occur
points: Half-filled and fully-filled subshells are extra stable, raising ionisation energy
N has 2p3 half-filled, so its ionisation energy exceeds O's
Be has 2s2 filled, so it exceeds B's

subtopics.name: Ionic versus atomic radius
points: Cations are smaller than their parent atoms; anions are larger
Isoelectronic species: more protons means smaller radius (Na+ < F- < O2-)
Across an isoelectronic series, radius falls as nuclear charge rises

class-11/chemistry/classification-of-ele.centralConcept: Modern periodic law and the long-form table

subtopics.name: Law and basis
points: Properties are periodic functions of atomic number (Moseley, 1913)
Atomic number is the number of protons, which fixes the electron configuration
The arrangement is therefore electronic, not mass-based

subtopics.name: Table structure
points: Seven periods and eighteen groups in the long form
Period number equals the highest principal quantum number occupied
Groups are numbered 1 to 18 under IUPAC convention

subtopics.name: Four blocks
points: s-block: groups 1-2 plus helium, filling ns
p-block: groups 13-18, filling np
d-block: groups 3-12, filling (n-1)d; f-block: filling (n-2)f

subtopics.name: Named families
points: Alkali metals (group 1), alkaline earth metals (group 2)
Halogens (group 17), noble gases (group 18)
Coinage metals (Cu, Ag, Au), volatile metals, metalloids along the B-Si-Ge-As-Sb-Te diagonal

subtopics.name: Reading the table as configurations
points: Group number for main-group elements relates to valence electron count
Anomalous configurations (Cr 3d5 4s1, Cu 3d10 4s1) arise from extra stability of half-filled and filled subshells
The table predicts chemistry before any experiment is done

class-11/chemistry/classification-of-ele.centralConcept: Classifying elements by group, period and block

subtopics.name: Three axes of classification
points: Group: vertical column, shared valence configuration
Period: horizontal row, shared outermost shell
Block: the subshell being filled

branches.topic: Level 2 — Core: the blocks in detail

subtopics.name: s and p blocks
points: s-block: highly reactive metals, low ionisation energy, form basic oxides
p-block: metals, metalloids and non-metals together, most varied chemistry
Metalloids sit on the diagonal and show both metallic and non-metallic behaviour

subtopics.name: d and f blocks
points: d-block: transition metals with variable oxidation states and coloured ions
f-block: lanthanides and actinides, filling inner f orbitals
Inner transition elements are chemically similar because f orbitals are shielded

subtopics.name: Why blocks matter
points: Block position predicts which subshell is chemically active
Explains why d-block elements show variable valency — s and d electrons are close in energy
Explains the lanthanide contraction and its effect on later transition metal radii

class-11/chemistry/classification-of-ele.centralConcept: IUPAC naming and numbering of the periodic table

subtopics.name: The 1-18 convention
points: IUPAC replaced the old IA-VIIIA and IB-VIIB labels with groups 1 to 18
Removes ambiguity between American and European conventions
Groups 1-2 and 13-18 are main group; 3-12 are transition

subtopics.name: Naming rules
points: New elements get a systematic name from their atomic number until confirmed
Roots: nil, un, bi, tri, quad, pent, hex, sept, oct, enn, plus the ending -ium
Example: element 118 was ununoctium before being named oganesson

subtopics.name: Group naming
points: Trivial names persist: alkali metals, halogens, noble gases, chalcogens
IUPAC accepts both numeric and trivial names
Group 3 membership (Sc, Y, La/Ac versus Lu/Lr) remains debated

subtopics.name: Why standardisation matters
points: A single numbering allows unambiguous cross-referencing in literature
Systematic naming prevents priority disputes over new elements
IUPAC also sets atomic weight and isotope conventions

class-11/chemistry/classification-of-ele.centralConcept: Effective nuclear charge — the pull an electron actually feels

subtopics.name: Two charges
points: Nuclear charge Z is the actual number of protons
Effective nuclear charge Zeff is the net positive charge experienced by an electron after shielding
Zeff = Z - sigma, where sigma is the shielding constant

subtopics.name: Shielding
points: Inner electrons repel outer electrons and reduce the nuclear pull they feel
Core electrons shield almost completely; same-shell electrons shield poorly
Slater's rules give a practical way to estimate sigma

subtopics.name: Penetration
points: s electrons penetrate closer to the nucleus than p, which penetrates more than d
Greater penetration means less shielding and a lower energy for that orbital
Explains the order of orbital filling: 4s fills before 3d

subtopics.name: Explaining trends
points: Zeff increases across a period because Z rises while shielding stays roughly constant
Zeff increases only slightly down a group because shielding rises with Z
Atomic radius, ionisation energy and electronegativity all follow from Zeff

subtopics.name: Quantitative anchors
points: For hydrogen Zeff = Z = 1, with no shielding
For a 2s electron in lithium, Zeff is about 1.3 rather than 3
Sodium's 3s electron feels Zeff of roughly 2.2, not 11

subtopics.name: Atomic radius
points: Decreases across a period as Zeff rises
Increases down a group as new shells are added
Measured as covalent, metallic or van der Waals radius depending on the element

subtopics.name: Ionic radius
points: Cations are smaller than the parent atom; anions are larger
Isoelectronic series: radius falls as nuclear charge rises (Na+ < F- < O2-)
Higher charge on the same ion means smaller radius (Fe3+ < Fe2+)

subtopics.name: Ionisation energy
points: Energy to remove the most loosely bound electron from a gaseous atom
Increases across a period, decreases down a group
Successive ionisation energies always increase; large jumps reveal shell structure

subtopics.name: Electron affinity and electronegativity
points: Electron affinity is the energy change on adding an electron; more negative across a period
Electronegativity is the tendency to attract a shared pair; Pauling scale
Both increase across a period and decrease down a group

subtopics.name: Metallic character
points: Decreases across a period, increases down a group
Metals lose electrons readily; non-metals gain them
Metalloids show intermediate behaviour

subtopics.name: Anomalies to memorise
points: IE of Be > B and N > O because of filled and half-filled subshell stability
IE of Mg > Al and P > S for the same reason
Electron affinity of F is less negative than Cl because of small size and electron repulsion

subtopics.name: Unifying explanation
points: Every trend traces back to Zeff and to the distance of the valence electron from the nucleus
Subshell stability explains the exceptions
Learn the cause, not the list — the exceptions follow from it
